h1:
Nong Prajak
Udon Thani's lake in the city
intro: Nong Prajak Silpakhom is a large lake right in the middle of Udon Thani that locals just call "Nong Prajak," and it's been the city's landmark for years. Most first-time visitors leave with a photo next to the giant yellow duck floating out on the water, while locals come here almost every evening to walk, run, cycle, or just sit by the water with the family. A walking and running loop runs about 3.2 kilometres around the lake, there are pedal boats for rent, an island in the middle you can cross to by bridge, and once evening hits, the whole perimeter turns into a long stretch of food stalls. This is a real-visit guide to Nong Prajak, with hours and prices kept current.

blocks.html: Nong Prajak sits within Udon Thani city limits, just a few minutes from the city centre and the train station. It started as a natural marsh that was turned into a public park, named after Major General Prince Prajak Silpakhom, the founder of Udon Thani. The draw is simple: a big green space in the middle of the city that's free to enter every day. If you're in Udon for even a couple of days, you'll almost certainly pass through here at least once — whether you're into exercise, photography, or eating.

blocks.text: How to get to Nong Prajak and opening hours

blocks.html: Nong Prajak is central and very easy to reach. If you're staying in town, a songthaew (shared truck), a Grab, or a motorbike taxi will get you there in a few minutes. The park itself is an open space and is free to enter every day — no admission fee. People come at two times of day: early morning before the sun gets harsh, and from late afternoon (around 4pm) onward, when it cools off and the whole loop fills up with walkers and runners.

items: Location — central Udon Thani, near the train station and the city markets, just a few minutes from in-town accommodation.
Park hours — it's an open space, free to enter any day. The busiest and best-feeling times are early morning and evening (roughly 4pm onward).
Parking — there are several parking spots around the lake; weekend evenings get crowded and harder to park, so arriving before dusk is easier.
What's nearby — UD Town and the in-town food areas are very close, so it's easy to carry the evening on from here.

blocks.title: The best time to come
blocks.html: If you want a good shot of the yellow duck in soft light, come near sunset when the water is still and the sky looks great. If you'd rather run or walk without the heat, early morning before 7am is best — cooler air and the loop isn't packed yet.

blocks.text: The giant yellow duck, the city's landmark

blocks.html: The thing that put Nong Prajak on the map is the giant yellow duck floating in the middle of the lake. Right now there's one big duck as the star plus several smaller ducks flanking it, and it's become the photo everyone visiting Udon ends up taking. The best angle is from the waterside that faces the duck — walk around until the duck sits right in the centre of your frame. In the evening the light is nicer and the still water gives you a reflection on the surface that beats a midday shot.

Beyond the duck, there are other photo spots scattered around the lake: the bridge over to the island, garden arbours, and waterside corners that open onto the wide lake view. You can wander the loop and shoot plenty of angles without rushing.

blocks.text: Walking, running and cycling the lake loop

blocks.html: For locals, the heart of Nong Prajak is the walking-and-running loop, about 3.2 kilometres around the lake. The surface is smooth, there's shade in stretches, and one lap is a solid distance. Come evening, the loop gets lively — runners, walkers, cyclists, and groups doing aerobics by the water. It's everyday life in Udon, and a lot of visitors end up loving the atmosphere.

items: Loop distance — about 3.2 km per lap, smooth and comfortable to walk or run, lit at night.
Peak times — late afternoon (4pm) to dusk is busiest, with waterside aerobics; early morning is quieter and cooler.
Cycling — you can cycle the loop, but the evening crowds mean you should ride slowly and watch for people crossing.
Water and restrooms — there are service points around the park, but weekend evenings get busy, so allow time for a queue.

blocks.title: Make the run count
blocks.html: If you're here to run, bring your own water or buy some from a stall around the lake before you start — a single lap is already over 3 km. In the evening, some sections share the same path between walkers and runners, so the grass-side lane tends to be clearer.

Another activity kids and families love is renting a pedal boat and heading out onto the lake. You get a view of the yellow duck and the park from the water that's different from walking the shore. The boats are pedal-powered for two or more people, charged by time slot at a friendly price, and they're ideal for taking kids out in the evening when the sun isn't strong.

In the middle of the lake there's an island you can reach by crossing a bridge. It's planted with flowering and ornamental plants and has a small garden to stroll through — a quiet spot to sit away from the bustle of the loop. You can cross over for photos and easily walk back to pick up the loop again.

items.name: Pedal-boat rental
items.blurb: Pedal boats for rent by the lakeshore. Cruise the middle of the water for views of the yellow duck and the park from angles you can't get on foot. Charged by time slot, great for kids and families.

items.name: The island
items.blurb: Cross the bridge onto the island, with a small garden, flowering and ornamental plants, and quiet corners to rest. A photo spot most people don't bother walking all the way into.

items.name: Yellow duck plaza
items.blurb: The waterside that faces the duck — the most popular photo spot. In the evening the light is lovely and the water is still, giving you a reflection on the surface.

items.name: Exercise area
items.blurb: In the evening, aerobics groups and runners fill the loop. It's real Udon daily life — even just sitting and watching is pleasant.

blocks.text: Restaurants and evening food around the lake

blocks.html: Come evening, the area around Nong Prajak is a genuine food destination — lakeside restaurants, chill-out spots, and snack carts scattered along the paths. Plenty of people finish their run or walk and head straight to eat. We've picked the restaurants and snacks you can find around the lake and the nearby area, focusing on places that are actually open and where locals actually eat.

items.name: Udon Miang Pla Joom
items.blurb: A well-known spot in the Nong Prajak area. The draw is its miang pla joom (fish hot pot) and punchy Isan dishes — a proper sit-down dinner. Both locals and visitors know it well. It's on Phibun Road near the lake.
items.meta: Isan / fish hot pot · open roughly 10:30am–8:30pm (closed Wed)

items.name: Krua Maitri (beside Nong Prajak)
items.blurb: A made-to-order and Isan restaurant right by the lake — bold, spicy flavours at local prices. Good for dinner after a lap around the lake, and a place the Udon review pages mention often.

items.name: Som tam and grilled chicken around the lake
items.blurb: The classic Udon pairing, found at several vendors around Nong Prajak: spicy papaya salad and fragrant grilled chicken with sticky rice. An easy dinner you shouldn't skip.

items.name: Meatball and grilled-skewer carts
items.blurb: Snack carts along the lakeside paths: fried meatballs, grilled pork, Isan sausage. Grab some and eat as you wander and take in the view. Easy on the wallet.

items.name: Noodles and clear-broth soup around the lake
items.blurb: Lakeside noodle shops for when you want something warm and brothy in the evening. There are several to choose from — a light meal after a workout.

items.name: Cafés by Nong Prajak
items.blurb: Several new cafés and milk-tea shops have opened around the lake. Sip a coffee or an iced milk tea with a lake view — good for resting your legs before or after the loop.

items.name: Desserts — shaved ice and roti
items.blurb: Cool-down desserts around the lake: shaved ice, roti, and sweet treats from carts. Kids love them, and they round off dinner nicely.

items.name: Breakfast spots across from Nong Prajak
items.blurb: For early-morning runners: across the lake there are breakfast spots open from 5am — rice-noodle soup, congee, pan eggs, and bakeries. Fill up before or after your run.

blocks.title: Carry the evening on at UD Town
blocks.html: If you're still not done, hop from Nong Prajak to UD Town, an open-air market-mall in the city (open roughly 10am–10pm) with lots of food and places to sit. It's close by and an easy continuation from the lake — a popular evening plan for visitors to Udon.

items: Pick your time — evening has a great atmosphere but bigger crowds; early morning is shadier and quieter; midday is hot and harsh, so avoid it if you can.
What to wear — sneakers or running shoes if you plan to walk the loop; a hat and water help a lot before the sun goes down.
Cash — snack carts, pedal boats, and the small shops around the lake mostly take cash, so bring small notes.
Mosquito repellent at dusk — there are mosquitoes by the water at night, so if you're sitting down to a long meal, packing spray makes it more comfortable.
Check closing days — some popular places around the lake have a weekly day off, so check ahead if you've set your heart on a particular one.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: Nong Prajak isn't a flashy attraction with big rides. Its strengths are a pretty lake in the middle of the city, a relaxed atmosphere, and evening food. If you come expecting thrilling activities, you might find it underwhelming — but if you come to stroll, photograph the yellow duck, and eat around the lake, you'll understand why locals come here every evening.

faq.q: Is Nong Prajak free, and what are the hours?
faq.a: It's free every day with no admission — it's an open public park. People mostly come early in the morning before the sun gets harsh, and from late afternoon (4pm) onward when it cools off and the whole loop fills up with walkers and runners.

faq.q: How long is the running loop around Nong Prajak?
faq.a: The walking-and-running loop is about 3.2 kilometres per lap, smooth and lit at night. One lap is a solid distance for a run or walk. In the evening you'll find runners, walkers, cyclists, and waterside aerobics groups.

faq.q: How do you rent a pedal boat at Nong Prajak, and how much is it?
faq.a: There are pedal boats for rent along the lakeshore, charged by time slot at a friendly price. You can cruise out for views of the yellow duck and the island from the water — ideal for taking kids and families out in the evening when the sun isn't strong.

faq.q: What's there to eat around Nong Prajak in the evening?
faq.a: Plenty — lakeside restaurants like Udon Miang Pla Joom and Krua Maitri, som tam and grilled chicken, noodles, meatball and grilled-skewer carts, cafés, and desserts. Many people stop to eat right after walking or running. If you're still not done, you can move on to UD Town in the city.

faq.q: What's the best angle to photograph the giant yellow duck at Nong Prajak?
faq.a: Shoot from the waterside that faces the duck. Near sunset the light is soft and the water is still, giving you a reflection of the duck on the surface that beats a midday shot. Early morning is also great and has fewer people.
